item.title: Red counties with data center projects swung away from GOP in midterms, analysis finds
item.description: Humans First's Amy Kremer warns data centers are driving voters away from Republicans as local control and property rights fuel community backlash.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: A new analysis from a conservative AI safety group found that deep-red counties with large data centers or proposed projects shifted further toward Democrats in last week's midterm elections than comparable counties without such projects.

Humans First’s analysis, obtained by Fox News Digital, examined public election returns and data-center project records in 1,540 counties across 16 states. The memo used several comparisons to measure what the group describes as a "data center penalty." Across all counties examined, those hosting large data centers shifted an additional 2.2 percentage points toward Democrats compared with non-host counties in the same states. The pattern appeared in 14 of the 16 states and 25 of the 27 governor and Senate races examined.

Restricting the analysis to deep-red counties — those President Donald Trump won by at least 20 points in 2024 — produced a 2.1-point raw gap between counties hosting large data centers and comparable counties without projects.

Among deep-red counties with projects still in the proposal stage, the gap was 1.1 percentage points after accounting for past voting patterns, rural or urban status, population size, racial and ethnic makeup and recent voting trends.

TEA PARTY FOUNDER LAUNCHES NATIONWIDE 'DATA CENTER REVOLT' AGAINST AI DATA CENTER EXPANSION

The group identified 114 proposed large data center projects across 92 deep-red counties, potentially setting up more local fights.

The memo found that Republican vote totals fell an additional 1.1% in deep-red host counties compared with comparable counties without large data centers, while Democratic vote totals showed no significant change.

The memo cautioned that its findings show an association rather than proof that data centers caused voters to change their behavior. County-level results also cannot determine whether Republicans switched their votes or simply stayed home.

"Our analysis looked at how counties with data centers voted and how those counties moved to the left," Humans First Chairwoman Amy Kremer told Fox News Digital.

"I think this happened for the reason I’ve been warning conservatives and Republicans about for some time: People engage politically when issues affect them personally. There’s nothing more personal than your pocketbook, your health care, your kids and family, your home and your community. A data center involves all of those things, which is why I believe these counties moved away from Republicans," she continued.

Humans First’s September "Data Center Revolt" bus tour made 35 stops in 27 states, including 14 stops in the states covered by the analysis. Nine of those stops were in deep-red counties, all of which hosted a large data center project. Those nine counties shifted 2.2 points further toward Democrats after the analysis accounted for its controls, compared with a 0.75-point shift among deep-red host counties overall. The group said those same nine counties showed no comparable gap from 2020 to 2024.

The findings do not establish whether the group's visits influenced voting behavior or whether those counties already had stronger opposition to data center development.

Separately, voters favored restrictions on data center development or rejected measures supporting such projects in 46 of 47 local data center ballot measures in 2026, according to Ballotpedia. The measures included different types of proposals, including restrictions on development and advisory questions.

Kremer said this is a local control issue, stressing that Republicans should focus on protecting property rights and ensuring people have control over how things affect their lives.

"Whether you’re talking about AI technology or the infrastructure needed to build AI data centers, the American people have not had a seat at the table," Kremer said. "They haven’t had a say in how the technology affects them or how the data center buildout affects their communities. In many places across the country, developers and companies have gone in and cut deals behind closed doors, under a cloak of darkness, using nondisclosure agreements and shell companies. By the time people in the community find out about the project, it’s too late to stop it."

"These projects affect the quality of life and how much money people have. They can increase the cost of electricity and water, while tax abatements are given to trillion-dollar companies — some of the wealthiest companies in the world. That is money coming out of the pockets of the American people," she continued.

Kremer added, "When you talk about Iran and gas prices, tariffs and now the AI data center buildout, all of these costs are coming out of people’s pockets. That’s when people engage politically, and I think that’s what we saw last Tuesday."

The concerns come amid a broader debate over how data centers should pay for the electricity and grid infrastructure they require. The Energy Department estimates data centers used 4.7% of U.S. electricity in 2024 and, in its reference case, could account for 11.8% by 2030. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has directed regional grid operators to address safeguards against shifting the costs of serving large electricity users onto other customers. Those developments do not establish that data centers caused higher household rates in the counties examined by Humans First.

Tax incentives also vary by state. The National Conference of State Legislatures reported that at least 38 states offer incentives specifically for data centers, including equipment-tax exemptions and, in some states, exemptions involving electricity or property taxes. The Data Center Coalition, an industry trade group, says such incentives are similar to those offered to other capital-intensive industries and argues that data centers generate jobs, investment and tax revenue.

Humans First does not support a nationwide or statewide moratorium on data centers, but Kremer said individual communities should be free to approve or reject projects.

DATA CENTERS FORGOT THE CONSUMER — AND THAT COULD COST AMERICA THE AI RACE

"If a community comes together and votes for a moratorium, that is its prerogative. If a community wants a data center, that is its prerogative as well. It is all about local control," she said.

Kremer said she learned that people engage more when it comes to issues that affect them personally, noting that data centers "encompass all of those issues."

"Whether you’re talking about pocketbook issues, health care, kids and family, or your home and community, the data center battle is a physical manifestation of all those concerns," she said. "When it comes to the economic impact on their communities, I think data centers absolutely played a role in the election."

"I hope we can get on the right page and give local control back to communities. People should have a say in how they live and what goes into their communities. That is very personal, and I hope we can move in that direction," Kremer added.

item.title: Troy Aikman pokes fun at ESPN contract standoff during Bills-Vikings Monday Night Football broadcast
item.description: Troy Aikman's diamond chain quip on Monday Night Football nodded at his stalled ESPN contract talks during the Bills' dominant 23-6 rout of Minnesota.
item.content:encoded:
Monday Night Football has recently felt like The Troy Aikman Show as the lead analyst wrestles with ESPN for a new contract, a stalemate that has reportedly created friction with booth partner Joe Buck.

Aikman nodded to the standoff during the Week 9 matchup between the Buffalo Bills and Minnesota Vikings.

Eyeing Justin Jefferson's heavily iced-out diamond chains, Aikman deadpanned, "I'm guessing that's insured. I cannot imagine wearing that on a football field. Can't imagine wearing it, period."

CHARLES BARKLEY WEIGHS IN ON THE FRICTION IN THE 'MONDAY NIGHT FOOTBALL' BROADCAST BOOTH

He then cracked that he might buy something similar, "if somebody would loan me some money ... "

ESPN paused negotiations after Aikman's camp sought a market-resetting extension near $30 million per year. Tensions reportedly deepened because Aikman expected a deal before reaching his walk year, especially after Buck secured a six-year, $108 million extension. With contract talks tabled, sports television’s longest-running broadcast partnership faces an uncertain future beyond this season.

ESPN ALLOWING TROY AIKMAN TO WALK AWAY FROM JOE BUCK BOOTH WOULD MAKE NO SENSE | BOBBY BURACK

Prior to Monday, Aikman, 59, hadn't let his expiring deal or Bristol's boardroom standoff bleed into the broadcast.

Whatever ESPN pays Aikman, it wasn't enough to sit through sixty minutes of Minnesota's offense. The Bills beat the Vikings, 23-6.

The Vikes benched Carson Wentz with four minutes left, turning to backup Max Brosmer. Wentz managed just three passing yards in the first quarter, finishing with an 8.9 passer rating, 81 yards passing and three turnovers (two INTs, lost fumble). He fell to Buffalo's pass rush and turned Justin Jefferson into a ghost. Jefferson finished with three catches for 58 yards.

Aikman didn't sugarcoat Minnesota’s cratered offense. "I don't know how you fix it," he said.

Lost in the collapse was a valiant effort by Minnesota's defense, which sacked Josh Allen four times.

The win moves the Bills to 7-1 before heading to East Rutherford to face the New York Jets, while the 6-2 Vikings must sort out their quarterback mess before a Week 10 trip to Lambeau Field against the Green Bay Packers.

item.title: U.S. Air Force mom surprises family on turf at Vikings-Bills game following 473-day overseas deployment
item.description: A military homecoming stunned Master Sergeant Kelsey McLeod's daughters at U.S. Bank Stadium as the Minnesota Vikings hosted the Buffalo Bills.
item.content:encoded:
Minnesota Vikings home fans got every bit of their money’s worth out of Monday night's football festivities, with U.S. Bank Stadium putting on a show to complement the primetime showdown against the Buffalo Bills.

During an early break in play, the NFL presented its signature "Salute to Service" moment at midfield. Standing on the turf were the two daughters and parents of Master Sergeant Kelsey McLeod, who was in attendance to surprise her family.

McLeod walked out from behind them as the stadium cameras caught her daughters turning around. The girls were in disbelief before sprinting into their mother's arms.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Her parents joined seconds later, embracing the returning service member for the first time in an astounding 473 days following her overseas tour in Korea.

An ovation grew from the roughly 66,000 fans in attendance, with players and coaches on both sidelines pausing to watch the heartwarming scene.

The energy carried into halftime as Minnesota officially inducted legendary running back Adrian Peterson into the Vikings Ring of Honor as its 29th member. Peterson, the franchise's all-time leading rusher, came out, and it was a shot of adrenaline for the Vikings faithful.

WNBA star Olivia Miles was also spotted on the turf in an unexpected cameo, patrolling the sidelines as a guest celebrity photographer with her camera in hand.

item.title: Philly DSA decries backlash over boycott targeting Jewish eateries
item.description: Philadelphia DSA condemned backlash against the bike boycott targeting Jewish-owned restaurants, calling criticism "bad-faith" attempts to "silence dissent."
item.content:encoded:
Philadelphia Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) released a statement Sunday condemning the backlash against a recent boycott ride targeting pro-Israel and Jewish local restaurant owners, calling it an act of "political repression of anti-Zionism."

Last week, the organizations Philly Bike On Your Left, Philly Writers Against the War on Gaza, Boycott CookNSolo and Philly Solidarity Calendar shared a flier promoting the bicycle boycott event, targeting at least six restaurants by name in Philadelphia's Rittenhouse Square.

The event received widespread condemnation from city and state leadership, particularly after it was scheduled on the eve of the anniversary of Kristallnacht, the 1938 Nazi pogrom against Jews in Germany and Austria marked by widespread anti-Jewish violence.

PHILADELPHIA 'BOYCOTT RIDE' TARGETING JEWISH BUSINESSES DRAWS CONDEMNATION FROM CITY, STATE LEADERSHIP

On the day of the boycott, Philly DSA attacked elected officials' statements, calling them "bad-faith" and "dangerous" for accusing critics of antisemitism.

"From the Senator [John] Fetterman and Congressman [Brendan] Boyle to Governor [Josh] Shapiro, Mayor [Cherelle] Parker, and Council President [Kenyatta] Johnson, politicians have joined a chorus of bad-faith and dangerous conflation of antisemitism with anti-Zionism and invoking comparisons to the Kristallnacht that trivialize trauma and suppress political speech," the group said in a statement. "These condemnations were not good-faith conversations about tactics."

Philly DSA clarified in its statement that it did not organize or endorse the boycott but accused city and state leaders of attempting "to delegitimize and chill acts of solidarity in the fight for Palestinian liberation" through "an unacceptable use of political power." The group also claimed that elected officials were likely pressured into their statements by "Zionist" organizations.

THE ANTISEMITISM HORSESHOE IS PLAYING OUT IN REAL TIME — FROM NEW YORK TO PARIS AND BEYOND

"We know that organized Zionist lobbying groups actively and intensely pressure elected officials, including our own elected socialists, to issue these condemnations, manufacturing political controversy that shifts attention away from Israel's actions and toward those organizing in solidarity with Palestine," the statement read.

Philly DSA emphasized that it was not antisemitic and rejected the framing of protests like the boycott as such.

"Jewish businesses and shops belong in Philadelphia: challenges to the violence of Zionist ideology do not dull this commitment to Jewish safety and belonging. DSA stands up and fights back against antisemitism, as we do for the dignity of all working people," the statement read.

In a comment to Fox News Digital, Philly DSA stood by its original statement. Parker's and Johnson's offices also stood by their original statements condemning the boycott. 

Shapiro spokesperson Rosie Lapowsky referred to a previous statement released by the governor's office on the boycott.

"The Shapiro Administration is aware of this planned protest and the Pennsylvania State Police is engaged with our local partners to ensure the safety and well-being of our neighbors in Philadelphia, Lapowsky said last week. "This bike ride, masquerading as a protest to advance the cause of justice, is nothing more than blatant antisemitism designed to intimidate and drive Jewish businesses out of our communities, and there is no place for that in our Commonwealth."

JEWISH TEENS PREPARE TO COMBAT ANTISEMITISM ON CAMPUS WITH HISTORY, HUMOR AND COURAGE

Fox News Digital also reached out to Fetterman's and Boyle's offices for comment.

On Sunday, hundreds of Jewish and pro-Israel community members turned out to oppose the demonstration, with heated exchanges unfolding across several city blocks. Dozens of diners also lined up outside the targeted restaurants in a show of solidarity with the Jewish-owned businesses.

Several Jewish and pro-Israel organizations, including the Israeli-American Council (IAC), also spoke out in defense of the targeted restaurants and encouraged others to do the same.

"When we heard about a ride taking place on the eve of the anniversary of Kristallnacht, we could not help but think about history and tell ourselves: we will not let this happen again. Today, we stand together, and we will not let anyone threaten our community," the IAC said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "This ride does not target a government or a policy. Its stated goal is to drive businesses owned by Zionists out of the city, as if being a Zionist were criminal or illegitimate. It targets six businesses whose owners are Jewish. When people publish a list of Jewish businesses and organize to drive them out of a city, we know from history what that is."

item.title: Rams coach Sean McVay 'kicking himself' after Puka Nacua's knee injury on final play likely lands him on IR
item.description: Sean McVay said he's "kicking himself" over the final play that left Puka Nacua with knee and turf toe injuries likely sending him to injured reserve.
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams’ injury woes continue, as wide receiver Puka Nacua is very likely heading to the injured reserve with an MCL and PCL sprain in his right leg, as well as turf toe.

And head coach Sean McVay admitted he’s "kicking himself" after Nacua’s knee ailments occurred on the final play of Sunday’s game where the Rams were leading the Washington Commanders.

"I'd be lying to you if I said I haven't questioned the decision-making on that last play over and over in my head of what could have been another option that you felt like could have gotten a conversion, and maybe ended the game that would've led to him not taking a violent hit to his right knee," McVay explained to reporters on Monday, per ESPN.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"And so, it's stuff that I feel tremendous responsibility for, and we've got to be able to figure out how to protect these guys while also putting them in positions that help our team and allow them to be able to shine."

Nacua was given a hand-off on a third-down play where the Rams were trying to end the game. He rushed for five yards, but he took a massive hit and stayed down on the ground longer than expected before walking off on his full power.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

But McVay revealed that Nacua will be missing a good chunk of time, and this is a team that’s already ailing at receiver with Davante Adams out for quite a while with a hamstring tear in Week 6 against the Arizona Cardinals.

If Nacua officially hits the IR as McVay indicated, he would be forced to miss the next four games for Los Angeles, which include matchups with the Cardinals, Green Bay Packers, Kansas City Chiefs and San Francisco 49ers.

With their top two receivers on the shelf, McVay said the Rams would "look at all avenues," including a potential trade before the Nov. 10, 4 p.m. ET NFL deadline, to add a receiver that quarterback Matthew Stafford could utilize.

Nacua is an obvious loss for this offense, as Stafford feels very comfortable giving him the ball no matter where he is on the field. Even missing Weeks 2 and 3 with a hip injury, Nacua has 70 catches for 715 yards and four touchdowns.

Those 70 receptions are the most for a player through their first seven games in NFL history.

This isn’t at all how the Rams, and the football world for that matter, saw their 2026 season unfolding with a 5-4 record after Week 9. But injuries to players like Myles Garrett, Aaron Donald, Jaylen Watson and many others have led McVay and his coaching staff to be creative in filling the gaps.

If the season were to end today, the Rams would not be in a playoff spot, and they are among teams with the hardest schedule moving forward. So, that creativity by McVay and others will be forced for weeks to come.

But this is an injury McVay can’t let himself off the hook for.

item.title: Philadelphia Eagles hit rock bottom as coach Nick Sirianni denies flipping off home fans
item.description: Nick Sirianni denied flipping off Philadelphia Eagles fans after a viral clip surfaced following the team's seventh straight loss to the New York Giants.
item.content:encoded:
Things have gone completely off the rails in Philly.

The Philadelphia Eagles sit at 2-7, and Nick Sirianni is defending himself against accusations of giving Eagles fans the bird.

Sunday’s 19-11 divisional loss against the New York Giants was bad enough on its own. New York had not won in South Philly since 2013, and the loss marked seven straight for an Eagles squad in free fall.

EAGLES HEAD COACH SAYS HE'D NEED TO BE A BETTER ACTOR THAN JOEY TRIBBIANI TO TONE DOWN HIS BEHAVIOR

Right after the final whistle, cameras caught Sirianni walking off with security chief Big Dom, appearing to raise his right middle finger toward booing fans.

Failing to stack up wins is one thing. Turning the home crowd into your enemy is the quickest way to get run out of town.

Asked about it Monday, Sirianni flatly denied flipping off the home fans.

"Absolutely not," Sirianni said. "That was a surprise to me. Absolutely not."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Sirianni has always been a loose cannon. Fans loved it when he was barking at road crowds in Kansas City and Indianapolis or jawing at opposing sidelines. He even caught flak for cupping his ear at the Linc during an ugly win over Cleveland. Taunting outside haters works when you're winning, but picking fights with paying hometown customers during a collapse is pure self-sabotage.

The offense is running on fumes without the retired Lane Johnson and with Jalen Hurts sidelined.

JALEN HURTS TO REPORTEDLY MISS REMAINDER OF NFL SEASON AFTER BLOOD CLOTS FOUND IN QUARTERBACK'S LUNGS

Interim starting Eagles QB Joe Milton had an expectedly ugly afternoon, throwing 18-of-34 for 169 yards, coughing up a lost fumble, and taking seven sacks, including three from Giants rookie linebacker Arvell Reese.

Across the field, a physical, Harbaugh-led Giants squad looks ready to take the NFC East. New York rotated J.J. McCarthy on the ground to move the chains and let Jameis Winston punch in the go-ahead score.

GIANTS STAR WIDEOUT BLASTS ANALYST FOR QUESTIONING SIDELINE BEHAVIOR DURING WIN AGAINST EAGLES

In the aftermath of the loss, Eagles general manager Howie Roseman hit the fire-sale button, trading defensive tackle Jordan Davis to Jacksonville on Monday for first and second-round picks. Philadelphia now holds 10 selections in the top two rounds over the next three drafts.

The future draft capital is loaded for tomorrow, but the present state of the Eagles is a complete disaster.

item.title: College Football Playoff committee executive admits they don't care fans are against 24-team playoff
item.description: The College Football Playoff expands to 24 teams by 2027-2028, but Executive Director Rich Clark acknowledged fans overwhelmingly oppose the change.
item.content:encoded:
Monday made what was long rumored official: we're moving to a 24-team College Football Playoff starting in the 2027-2028 season.

The reaction from most fans, commentators, analysts as well as many coaches and people within the sport, can be summed up in one word: why?

As recently as 2023, the playoff was four teams. The smaller field ensured that the best of the best would compete for a title. Only one-loss or undefeated teams had a chance at postseason glory ... well, unless you were an undefeated Florida State team.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF EXPANDING TO 24 TEAMS IN 2027, WITH MORE GAMES COMING TO CAMPUSES ACROSS THE COUNTRY

Then, in 2024, we moved to a 12-team format, which offered more opportunity for teams to change their season. The 2024-2025 Ohio State Buckeyes were a perfect example, losing the final game of the season before roaring back to life and steamrolling their way through to a championship.

The 12-team format has generally been well liked; it's a solid balance of maintaining the exclusivity of the tournament, while adding more big postseason games on campuses and mostly preserving bowl season and the importance of the regular season. While the upcoming 2026-2027 version of the playoff will be just the third under the expanded format, we're already moving on to even more teams. Somehow.

24 teams essentially means the end of meaningful bowl games. With a bowl field so diluted by the increase in playoff participants, the remaining bowls will be picking up scraps. Major conference championship games are set to become a thing of the past.

The regular season, long the best in sports, will be significantly less meaningful. Not only will three losses not be enough to keep teams out, there's a strong chance that four or potentially even five loss teams (from the SEC) will be in the 24-team playoff. This might mean more scheduled games between big programs, since they'll no longer be concerned about a single loss hurting their chances, but if it doesn't, the sport will have sacrificed the regular season almost entirely.

Which again, raises the all-important question: who wanted this? Who was asking for it? Why is it even happening?

The answer is money, money and money. The Big Ten led the charge for more playoff spots, and other conferences and groups eventually fell in line. The SEC, long the hold out, caved, presumably because commissioner Greg Sankey realized he could start campaigning for all 16 conference teams to reach the playoff each season.

Obviously, more playoff games means more money coming from the broadcast partner, ESPN. More teams will have late-season home games with a potential "playoff appearance" on the line. Then be able to sell expensive home playoff game tickets to their fans. Coaches now have a lower bar to claim a successful season. And boosters can see a return on investment instead of seeing their money go towards reaching the Pop-Tarts Bowl.

The one group missing here? Fans. As usual. Fans weren't asking for this, and surveys have shown that they overwhelmingly don't want it. Unsurprisingly, it's happening anyway. And in a news conference announcing the change, Executive Director Rich Clark explained why: the playoff committee doesn't care.

BIG TEN CONFERENCE COMMISSIONER GIVES TONE DEAF STATEMENT ABOUT 24-TEAM COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF

Clark said on the call that changes brought about by the 24-team field will be beneficial for the sport, and most importantly, the business school executive's new favorite word: "stakeholders."

"New scheduling standards will incentivize institutions to schedule more compelling non-conference matchups during the regular season, and 16 Playoff games will now be played on campuses, bringing Playoff football to more students and local fans," Clark said. "Finally, our commitment as the CFP administration and staff, we will make the 24-team Playoff spectacular for the fans, for the student-athletes, for the institutions, and for all our stakeholders."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Clark answered a few questions, saying that the committee will evaluate and encourage strong schedules, and teams will be required to play 10 games against teams from Power 4 conferences. That's all well and good. But what came next was frustrating and a bit emblematic of how this whole process has played out.

One reporter asked Clark about fan opinion, saying "the online segment of the fan base seems to be maybe against this," and wondered how Clark thought it would be "received by fans." Here's what he said:

"We're aware of the fan sentiment and that many fans aren't in favor of expansion," Clark responded. "That was certainly weighed into the decision. It was considered. Ultimately we just need to make a spectacular Playoff. I mean, the CFP has a responsibility to our fans, they're the lifeblood of college football. We owe it to them to make this great. That really is our intent. We appreciate our fans. We did take into account their sentiment. That was rolled into this decision. But we decided to move forward with it."

Ah. Yes. We know fans don't want it, we just didn't care and did it anyway because it made more money. Perfection.

Obviously, that's the real explanation for why they decided to "move forward" anyway. Fans are dead last when it comes to priorities among the leadership in college football. A "spectacular playoff" doesn't require 24 teams, in fact, it's more likely to dilute it.

In 2025-2026, for example, several games between P4 and G6 teams were widely decried as being non-competitive. Ole Miss blew out Tulane 41-10 and Oregon handled James Madison 51-34. Even in the 2024-2025 playoff, ESPN's Kirk Herbstreit went on a rant decrying the Indiana Hoosiers reaching the 12-team field when they lost 27-17. In a 24-team format, how bad will that 24th team be?

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

Probably not great!

But this is what happens in modern college football; those in charge focus exclusively on short-term financial success over long-term health. Fans come last. Money comes first. At least this time they're admitting it.

item.title: NTSB recovers cockpit voice recorder from Learjet crash site in Florida
item.description: The NTSB recovered the cockpit voice recorder from the Learjet 60 crash site near Greenacres, Florida, as investigators probe the cause of the incident.
item.content:encoded:
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) announced on Monday that it has recovered the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) of the Learjet 60 that crashed last week near Greenacres, Florida, killing all nine people on board.

"NTSB investigators have recovered the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) of the Learjet 60 that crashed on Nov. 1 near Greenacres, Florida," the NTSB said on X.

The CVR was found at the location of the initial impact​, according to the NTSB.

The NTSB said the CVR is being evaluated in the board's Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, D.C.

TIMELINE OF LEARJET CRASH THAT KILLED AUSTIN FAMILY TRACES FINAL MINUTES FROM TAKEOFF TO FLORIDA PLUNGE

The excavation work at the impact site has been completed.

This comes after investigators said on Friday that they recovered part of an engine from the Learjet.

Crews started excavating the site on Wednesday after utility workers had drained water and cleared other hazards, the NTSB said.

Once investigators began digging, they found a part of one engine, the board said.

Earlier last week, investigators recovered the left tail elevator, which controls the jet's pitch, in three separate pieces. One of them was found nearly four miles from where the Learjet 60 crashed.

FLORIDA PLANE CRASH VICTIMS IDENTIFIED AFTER 9 PEOPLE KILLED IN FIERY WRECK

"Even small pieces of the wreckage may contain important evidence that could help investigators determine what happened," the agency wrote last week on X.

The Learjet 60 left Austin-Bergstrom International Airport around 10:37 a.m. on Sunday, bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas. The aircraft plunged into the ground in Palm Beach County shortly before 1 p.m., killing everyone aboard.

Austin tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, 45, was killed in the crash alongside his wife, Helen Sharp, 40, their children, Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, the children's nanny, Anita Maria Cetina, and couple Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr.

Heavy rain and thunderstorms were reported across South Florida when the Learjet crashed. Investigators said the weather will be a major focus of their probe.

At about 41,000 feet, an air traffic controller told the flight crew that moderate precipitation was roughly five miles away and said they could move either left or right, stressing that the turn toward Freeport in the Bahamas "looks pretty bad."

The crew was then instructed to fly to a waypoint near Naples, Florida. The crew made a deviation toward Palm Beach County and reported that weather conditions were deteriorating. The crew told air traffic control that there was icing and turbulence, asking the controller if there was a "better ride" ahead.

 Fox News' Adam Sabes contributed to this report.

item.title: Democrats could create 'angry' 'single-issue' voters in 2028 if they remove school choice, CEO warns
item.description: The CEO of America's largest school choice group warns Democrats that abolishing voucher programs could spark a massive voter backlash in 2028.
item.content:encoded:
The CEO of America’s largest school choice advocacy organization is warning Democrats that abolishing existing universal school choice programs could trigger a major voter backlash in the 2028 elections.

"Put yourself into the shoes of a lower-income mother who is a single parent. She has two or three kids that now just got access into a great private school or a great homeschooling environment that she couldn't afford otherwise without a state program like in Texas, and suddenly, the new wave of people that maybe she even voted for is saying, 'I want to take those options away from your kid immediately and put them back into the school that they've hated,'" American Federation for Children CEO Tommy Schultz told Fox News Digital. "That you've been begging the school district to change policies about … You're now going to tell them you got to go back to that school? They're going to become a single-issue voter in 2028 and vote you out of office."

"I think a lot of these folks that just won office need to be really careful with trying to threaten taking away a family from an educational setting that their kids are thriving in that they're loving, that they're feeling safe in," he added. "That's fundamentally what's at issue here."

DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT

Schultz’s comments followed recent midterm election gains by Democrats that have put landmark Republican education policies into question. Republican governors across the country previously passed universal school choice and parental rights measures as post-COVID culture war debates intensified and enrollments declined in major metropolitan public school districts.

In Texas, Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa signaled her intent to reverse school choice expansion upon taking office.

11TH-HOUR POWER PLAY TARGETS INCOMING DEM GOVERNOR AFTER HISTORIC GOP DEFEAT

"It is a victory for the parents of Texas. We are taking our children’s education back from a government that has failed them," Hinojosa said during her victory speech. "Schools will not be taken out of our control, shuttered or suffocated. Being a parent is hard enough without carrying the burdens of a government’s failures. To the children of Texas: Your schools will not close."

The renewed clash over vouchers comes as major urban districts navigate shifting enrollment dynamics. Big-city public school systems across the nation have struggled to retain students as families seek alternative options outside their neighborhood assignments.

NUMBER OF K-12 PUBLIC SCHOOL STUDENTS HAS DECLINED IN MORE THAN HALF OF STATES, REPORT INDICATES

In Texas, for example, the Houston Independent School District board previously voted unanimously to close 12 campuses, citing declining enrollment.

"On day one, I will fire [Texas Education Agency Commissioner] Mike Morath, and we will work tirelessly to repair the damage of the Texas voucher scam, and end an era in which our schools are sold for parts," Hinojosa added during her victory remarks.

A BLUE WAVE IN GOVERNORS' MANSIONS COULD HURT FAMILIES MORE THAN A BLUE CONGRESS

Voucher and school choice programs face similar legislative challenges following Democratic victories in states like Iowa, Georgia and Nevada.

Schultz predicted that attempts to roll back school choice legislation could ignite a new wave of parental rights activism. Conservative victories in school board races in recent cycles underscored how parents began paying closer attention to local governance, challenging progressive curricula, and voicing strong opposition to explicit content and LGBTQ-related books in classrooms.

MOMS FOR LIBERTY UNLEASHES AI WATCHDOG ON 13,000 SCHOOL DISTRICTS TO FLAG CONTROVERSIAL POLICIES BEFORE VOTES

Conservative political action committees have significantly expanded their footprint in local education contests since 2022. The Virginia-based American Principles Project (APP) first engaged in Florida school board races that year, funding attack ads targeting critical race theory and gender ideology. The APP and the 1776 Project PAC remain among the prominent conservative groups working to shape national education policy.

Since the COVID-19 pandemic, school board meetings have frequently turned into high-profile clashes over parental authority in public education. Schultz foresees similar grassroots pushback if choice options are eliminated.

DENVER MOTHER FIGHTS FOR HER DAUGHTER'S EDUCATION AS ADVOCATES MAKE NATIONWIDE SCHOOL CHOICE PUSH

"If you're going to take away something from parents that they're really loving—like especially something as emotional as the school that your kid is going to—they’re going to get quite angry," Schultz said. "That's where you've seen these movements, in Florida, where these parents rose up against candidates or even court cases where they tried to take hundreds of thousands of kids out of the schools they loved and put 'em back in the schools that they hated. They became single-issue voters."

The broader parental rights movement led several Republican governors to codify parental bills of rights in recent years. Political analysts frequently point to parental rights platforms as key drivers in the election campaigns of figures like former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.

TRUMP EDUCATION OFFICIAL SAYS SCHOOL CHOICE PROGRAM WILL PUT PRESSURE ON DEM-LED STATE

"If you look at the headlines from that 2018 race with Governor Ron DeSantis, the school choice moms tipped the Florida race for him," Schultz said. "That's the type of thing we're talking about that could happen to a lot of these candidates who maybe won on affordability, but they won maybe on small margins, particularly in these state legislative races."

"Don't overread your mandate to suddenly say, 'I want to wipe out a really popular program with parents,'" he added.

Hinojosa did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

item.title: Colts' Jonathan Taylor deserves to be sent to 'contender' if traded, former teammate says
item.description: Nick Foles said the Indianapolis Colts should trade Jonathan Taylor to a contender, but admits the rebuild-driven business decision pains him.
item.content:encoded:
NFL teams are coming down to the wire when it comes to the trade deadline, needing to make trades for the remainder of the season by 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday.

At this point, teams have positioned themselves as buyers or sellers, and the Indianapolis Colts are the latter. And all eyes are on them to see what happens with All-Pro running back Jonathan Taylor.

Will he remain in a Colts uniform for, at least, the rest of the year? Or will a contender finally hit the asking price needing to send him elsewhere?

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon, who gave the nod to trade guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner already, is reportedly taking calls on Taylor as well as quarterback Daniel Jones and wide receiver Josh Downs. But Taylor has been the cream of the trade buzz crop since the Colts cemented themselves as a team in rebuild mode.

So, should Irsay-Gordon and interim GM Ed Dodds pull the trigger on a Taylor trade? That question was posed to former Colts quarterback Nick Foles, who has been watching the situation unfold very closely, by OutKick during a recent interview look ahead to his role as an analyst on Netflix for the first-ever NFL Thanksgiving Eve game later this month.

"Man, now I have to put on a business mind, right?" he responded. "As a person who was his teammate, I would never trade him ‘cause I know just what he brings to the team as a leader and as a player. But as a personnel decision maker, he’s getting older as a running back, and if you can get something super value like a high draft pick for him – you are in rebuild. You’ve already shown that. I feel like you’re going to do it.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"That pains me to say."

If the Colts do decide to part ways with the 27-year-old running back, he did have one request.

"Please send Jonathan to a team that’s a contender," he said emphatically. "Give him that opportunity, right? Like he deserves that opportunity.

"If they do, he will be dearly missed in Indianapolis because of the quality of human being, teammate, and player he is. But I can definitely see her doing it from a business perspective in this rebuild to just get some draft capital."

If the Colts are going to trade Taylor, they reportedly want a steep asking price met – something like the San Francisco 49ers gave the Carolina Panthers for Christian McCaffrey. That was a second-, third, and fourth-round pick in 2023 and a 2024 fifth-round pick in the famous 2022 deadline deal.

A contender with that type of draft capital could justify the move knowing Taylor would be locked in through the 2028 season. It wouldn’t just be a trade for the 2026 campaign, but two years in the future before a possible extension.

Among the teams being aggressive on the trade market are the New York Giants, as the John Harbaugh-led squad owns the top spot in the NFC East in his first season there, and they could use an elite running back to add to their offense now and for the future. The Denver Broncos, Minnesota Vikings and others have been rumored to be in the Taylor market, but the clock is ticking and time is of the essence.

Who will bend first, if at all? This is why the deadline is so intriguing for NFL fans, including Foles who can’t wait to see where teams stack up after it.

Foles also can’t wait for his duties on Nov. 25 when he and fellow ex-pros Clay Matthews and Michael Irvin join Elle Duncan as part of the broadcast crew for the historic matchup between the Los Angeles Rams and Green Bay Packers. U2 will also celebrate 50 years together from the 50-yard line, as they perform at halftime with special guests during this new NFL holiday tradition.

Teams will look different at that point, though, and the coming weeks will show if those trade deadline moves paid off or not.

item.title: Knicks guard walks back comment about Taylor Swift being fake fan after Swifties, including his wife, attack
item.description: Tyler Kolek walked back his comments calling Taylor Swift the "fakest" courtside celebrity fan after fierce backlash from Swifties and the Knicks.
item.content:encoded:
Knicks guard Tyler Kolek knew the Swifties weren't going to appreciate him calling Taylor Swift the "fakest" celebrity fan that sits courtside. It wouldn’t matter if she actually was, that group will defend the singer no matter what.

He probably didn’t know his own franchise was going to throw him under the bus. They did, almost immediately after his comments started to circulate.

A spokesperson said in a statement to OutKick, "Taylor Swift has been a Knicks fan for many years, has a long history with Madison Square Garden, and we are incredibly appreciative of her support of the organization."

Now if anyone was going to have his back, it would be his girlfriend Lexi Sousa, right? While I'm sure she didn’t kick him out of the house over it, she didn’t exactly have his back either.

She reminded Kolek that he was one of the guys in attendance during the Era's Tour, who, it doesn’t sound like needed to be dragged there by his girlfriend. The heat from the Swifties, including his girlfriend, had him walk back the comment.

"It’s just a question that was asked for me, that maybe I answered in the wrong way. Take that on the chin. I love her music. We were just playing it five minutes ago, and I’m singing every word to every song. Nothing against her at all," he said after the Knicks win over the Cavs this weekend, according to the NY Post.

"People have been going back and sending me all this stuff about her coming to the games, and she was actually wearing a [No.] 13 jersey [of] Joakim Noah back in the day with Carmelo [Anthony]. That’s on me. I wasn’t up to date on my Taylor Swift Knicks fandom. So that’s on me."

NFL LEGEND EMMITT SMITH DEFENDS TAYLOR SWIFT AS HER PRESENCE AT GAMES DRAWS IRE OF FOOTBALL FANS

The fact that the Knicks wanted no part of the Swifties too is another piece of this that is hard for me to wrap my mind around. All I'm going to say is Tyler Kolek better bone up on his Kylie Jenner Knicks fandom.

She's done more for the Knicks than a lot of other fans, including Taylor Swift. Unlike Kolek, I'll stand by that.

You won't find my apologizing, because if you do, you'll end up doing things like Taylor Swift karaoke in the locker room.

item.title: Charlamagne tha God calls out Dave Chappelle's Kirk comments, wouldn't wish them 'on my worst enemy'
item.description: Charlamagne Tha God said on "The Breakfast Club" that he doesn't "find the humor" in Dave Chappelle's joke about feeling "better" after Charlie Kirk's assassination.
item.content:encoded:
Radio host Charlamagne tha God criticized comedian Dave Chappelle's joke about the assassination of Turning Point USA (TPUSA) founder Charlie Kirk on Monday.

Despite rules barring cell phones from the Madison Square Garden show, a video circulating on social media on Friday showed Chappelle appearing to make the remarks during his "Karmageddon" tour stop in New York City.

"I feel f----- up saying this. It’s scary being a public speaker. And I mean, look, ever since that guy, Charlie Kirk, got murdered, and I shouldn’t say this publicly, but, I feel better," Chappelle said.

'SNL' WEEKEND UPDATE ANCHOR CALLS REPUBLICANS SLURS, MOCKS CHARLIE KIRK IN STAND-UP SPECIAL

After playing the audio of his comments on his radio show "The Breakfast Club," Charlamagne immediately responded that he didn't "find the humor" in the comment.

"I don't find the humor in people getting clapped, okay?" Charlamagne said. "Any of us can be shot, and I don't want anybody getting shot because somebody disagrees with their opinion. So yeah, you have the freedom to, you know, joke and talk about whatever you want to joke and talk about, but personally I don't want to deal with the energy of that. Like I don't wish stuff like that on my worst enemy."

WELCH DOUBLES DOWN ON TPUSA FEUD, CALLS GROUP 'LOSERS' AFTER LAUGHING AT JOKE ABOUT KILLING CHARLIE KIRK AGAIN

Some of his co-hosts noted that the clip of Chappelle's comments was released without any additional context. Charlamagne agreed but remarked that it seemed like it was an "observation" made by Chappelle.

"It just sounded like he made an observation — at least from what that clip just played, that it was just like he felt better after Charlie Kirk got shot and killed," Charlamagne said.

PETE DAVIDSON SPARKS BACKLASH AFTER EXPLICIT JOKE ABOUT SLAIN CHARLIE KIRK DURING NETFLIX ROAST

Fox News Digital reached out to Charlamagne's and Chappelle's representatives for comment.

In his comments, Chappelle described not only feeling "better" after Kirk's death but also experiencing unexpected high spirits after the news.

"I just be driving around like, ‘Why am I in such a good mood? Oh!'" Chappelle remarked.

Chappelle received backlash across social media for what some commentators called a "sick" joke. In response to the viral video, TPUSA pointed Fox News Digital to Erika Kirk's statement on X, in which she wrote that treating the destruction of human life as a punchline is "disgusting."

"A culture that laughs at assassination is one of profound moral decay. It threatens the very foundation of our country and the principles that hold our democracy together. You do not have to agree with someone’s politics to recognize the value of their life. This should not be so hard," she wrote.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, TPUSA spokesperson Andrew Kolvet made similar comments, acknowledging people's freedom of speech but encouraging a level of decorum.

"We're not asking people to, you know, be evangelical Christians here. We're asking don't celebrate, condone or glorify political violence. Don't be happy when someone's assassinated. It's a very, very low bar. But if we don't keep it, then everything else falls apart," Kolvet said.

item.title: Bruce Springsteen fan club founders say political fights, El-Sayed endorsement led to shutdown: report
item.description: Bruce Springsteen's endorsement of Michigan's senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed proved the final straw for the Spring-Nuts fan club founders as group shutters.
item.content:encoded:
A Bruce Springsteen fan club couldn't escape the badlands and shuttered over political commentary.

Founded more than a decade ago, the "Spring-Nuts" Facebook group dedicated to The Boss noticed its 18,000 members were no longer focused on his music as they battled against "hateful" online discourse due to Springsteen's public stances and recent endorsement of Michigan's senator-elect, Abdul El-Sayed.

"As the world grew increasingly divisive, hostile, those tensions inevitably spilled into our little corner of the E Street world," founders Julie and Howie Chaz said in a statement posted on Sunday, Nov. 8, according to Asbury Park Press.

BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN SPARKS FAN FURY AFTER BACKING ABDUL EL-SAYED IN MICHIGAN SENATE RACE

"What should have been respectful differences of opinion too often deteriorated into personal attacks, bullying, insults, and some genuinely vile and hateful rhetoric."

Springsteen embarked on the "Land of Hope and Dreams" tour earlier this year with the E Street Band and legendary guitarist Tom Morello.

The 20-date tour across North America was slated in response to President Donald Trump and the "No Kings" protests.

BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN REIGNITES TRUMP FEUD, SAYS 'CRITICAL PATRIOTISM' DEFINES A PATRIOT

"We are living through dark, disturbing and dangerous times, but do not despair – the cavalry is coming," Springsteen said while announcing the tour on social media in February.

"We will be rocking your town in celebration and in defense of America – American democracy, American freedom, our American Constitution and our sacred American dream – all of which are under attack by our wannabe king and his rogue government in Washington, D.C."

He added, "Everyone, regardless of where you stand or what you believe in, is welcome – so come on out and join the United Free Republic of E Street Nation for an American spring of rock 'n' rebellion! I’ll see you there!"

"Spring-Nuts" founder Howie Chaz admitted that as Springsteen became "more outspoken about his politics," the group administrators were tasked with a "difficult balancing act" of respecting "his absolute right" while maintaining an ethical online community.

"How could we be a Bruce Springsteen fan community trying to protect that harmony and camaraderie and ignore messages and statements coming directly from the very artist who brought us all together," Howie said.

Springsteen's November endorsement of El-Sayed as "a fighter for our American Constitution" was the final straw for admins.

"Mr. Sayed campaigned with Hasan Piker who openly made horrific statements that America deserved 9/11," Howie said.

"After a Michigan synagogue was attacked back in March, obviously an act of terrorism, Sayed rationalized it by saying 'Hurt people hurt people' standing right next to the antisemitic streamer Hasan Piker who made the despicable 9/11 statement."

His endorsement was "deeply disappointing to us, given our concerns as proud Jews," Julie and Howie said.

"We certainly don't believe Bruce intended for his message to make fans feel unwelcome. But very unfortunately, some of his fans appointed themselves the gatekeepers of who was and wasn't worthy of belonging in the E Street community."

While the group's annual Seaside Serenade and Spring-Nuts podcasts will continue under a different name, the group will rebrand with a focus on music in general, Howie told the Asbury Park Press.

item.title: Man killed in fiery Kentucky jet crash told daughter of trouble in midair
item.description: Before he died, a Wisconsin father radioed his daughter about issues he was having after takeoff on Sunday, Nov. 8. Then his jet hit a ditch and caught fire in Kentucky.
item.content:encoded:
A 70-year-old Wisconsin man was killed in a fiery crash Sunday, Nov. 8, when his military-style jet plunged into a field in Mayfield, Kentucky, shortly after takeoff.

The accident turned a cross-country flight alongside his daughter into a sudden tragedy.

The pilot, identified as James Alan Michaels of Dousman, Wisconsin, and his 35-year-old daughter, Tonie Michaels, were flying separate L-39 Albatros jets. 

"The father and daughter were flying back to Wisconsin from Mississippi," the Graves County Sheriff's Office told Fox News Digital.

'WE NEED TO RETURN IMMEDIATELY,' FLIGHT CREW WARNS AS PILOT HEALTH EMERGENCY UNFOLDS

The pair had been at an air show and stopped at an airport in Mayfield to get fuel, the sheriff's office said.

After takeoff, "they were gaining altitude and the deceased ... said he was having issues," the sheriff's office said. "He was going to turn and go back to the airport."

Soon after, "he radioed ... that he was not going to be able to land," the sheriff's office said.

"We think he tried to land in an open field," the sheriff's office said.

However, at around 2:08 p.m., the plane went down just off Spence Chapel Road near Interstate 69 and Ky. 131. "It hit a ditch in that field," the sheriff's office said.

"The ditch seems to be the cause of the main impact," the sheriff's office said. "The plane caught fire and actually rolled."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

The pilot was the only person on the plane. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

The daughter soon arrived at the scene, the sheriff's office said. 

"She turned around and landed back at the airport. [Then] she started making phone calls."

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) told Fox News Digital that Sunday's crash occurred around 2:25 p.m. local time, though local authorities recorded the crash time slightly earlier, at 2:08 p.m.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said its investigators will lead the probe into the crash. 

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

An investigator was expected to arrive at the scene Monday evening to document the site and examine the aircraft before it's recovered to a secure facility for further evaluation, the NTSB said.

The NTSB said its investigations involve three primary areas: the pilot, the aircraft, and the operating environment. 

As part of the process, investigators will gather flight track data, air traffic control communications, aircraft maintenance records, witness statements and weather conditions, the agency said.

It said investigators will also review the pilot’s license, ratings, recency of flight experience and 72-hour background check to determine if any issues could have affected his ability to safely operate the flight.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

During the on-scene phase of the investigative process, the NTSB does not determine or speculate about the cause of the accident, the agency said.

A probable cause of the crash along with any contributing factors will be detailed in the final report, which is expected in 12 to 24 months, the NTSB said.

Sixteen years prior to this accident, the same father and daughter duo survived a small-plane crash in a remote area of Rocky Mountain National Park in Colorado, WBAY News Report said at the time.

On July 8, 2010, James Michaels was piloting a single-engine aircraft with his daughter as his passenger when they encountered a severe downdraft.

The pair crash-landed in heavy timber in Forest Canyon while flying toward Aspen, the National Park Service Summary Report via NTSB Docket previously said.

Both walked away from the 2010 crash with minor cuts and scratches. 

They used branches and the plane's sheared-off wreckage to build a shelter as they were stranded overnight during evening storms, The Denver Post reported at the time.

item.title: Trump renews call for Pete Rose pardon, saying MLB's all-time hits leader was 'mistreated'
item.description: Trump said he would pardon Pete Rose for federal tax charges, calling MLB's all-time hits leader "very mistreated" during a meeting with Dana White.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump is back saying he would pardon Major League Baseball’s all-time hits leader, the late Pete Rose, but not just for his gambling scandal that has him out of the National Baseball Hall of Fame to begin with.

He would’ve pardoned him in his capacity for federal tax charges he pleaded guilty to in April 1990.

Trump was alongside UFC CEO Dana White, whom the 47th president said he was "only kidding" about making his new press secretary on Truth Social over the weekend. Nonetheless, White flew to Washington D.C. to meet with Trump and field questions from reporters.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

He was asked about Pete Rose first, with the reporter referencing Trump’s consideration to pardon the baseball great in the past.

"I don’t advise the president on anything ever, but yeah, I think it’s fair. I think it’s fair to pardon Pete Rose. Yes," White responded.

Then, Trump jumped in.

"By the way, why does he need a pardon? He was not really convicted of a criminal – " Trump said before he was cut off by the reporter to provide clarity.

TRUMP SAYS HE WAS ‘ONLY KIDDING’ ABOUT MAKING DANA WHITE PRESS SECRETARY

"It was tax charges, sir," the reporter said.

"Oh, he did? I’d give Pete Rose a pardon," Trump responded. "I think Pete Rose was very mistreated. He had 4,200-and-some-odd hits, way ahead of anyone else. A record that can’t ever be broken. And he was caught gambling, and now it’s legal. But he was gambling on his own team, Dana. He wasn’t gambling against [his team] – that’s different.

"He was gambling. He shouldn’t have done it, but he went through 40 years of hell and they should be giving him a pardon. They should be getting him into the [National] Baseball Hall of Fame a long time ago. I spoke to the commissioner about it. He agreed to do it, and then he waited though, and Pete Rose died. So, it didn’t help him too much, but I would give Pete Rose a pardon. I would do that."

In March 2025, Trump took to Truth Social to say he would be "signing a complete pardon" of Rose, who had died the previous year before ever seeing himself in the Hall of Fame in Cooperstown, New York. Writers, though, had never been given the option to vote in the man with the most hits in MLB history (4,256) with the Baseball Writers Association of America (BBWAA) and Hall of Fame following suit with the league’s lifetime ban of Rose in 1989 for gambling.

But commissioner Rob Manfred lifted that ban of Rose and several other players posthumously from the ineligible list in May 2025, allowing the possibility for those players to be voted in. That has yet to happen.

Speaking with reporters back in May, Trump suggested Rose’s absence from the Hall was a "disservice."

"I think Pete Rose should have been in the Baseball Hall of Fame a long time ago," Trump said. "I think baseball did a great disservice by not respecting his achievements on the field."

Manfred admitted at an owners meeting in 2025 that Trump’s support for Rose was one of the many factors that went into the decision to lift him from the ineligible list.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"The president was one of a number of voices that was supportive of the idea that this was the right decision," Manfred said in May 2025. "Obviously, I have respect for the office, and the advice that he gave I paid attention to, but I had a lot of other people that were weighing in on the topic as well."

Major League Baseball itself does not control who gets into the Hall of Fame; the baseball writers vote initially, while other committees to get players in further down the road are made by the Hall itself, not the league.

Rose died last September at the age of 83 from hypertensive and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

Nicknamed "Charlie Hustle" for his relentless drive when on the diamond, Rose was league MVP in 1973, a 17-time All-Star, three-time batting title winner, Rookie of the Year and World Series MVP.

Despite his 4,256 career hits, he became a polarizing figure when the news of his gambling on baseball rocked the sports world.

Rose tried to apply for reinstatement to Major League Baseball on several occasions but was always denied. MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred denied one in 2015, saying that Rose did not take responsibility for his actions and didn’t understand the damage he had caused while betting on the game.

Rose applied for reinstatement in 2020 and 2022, especially with legalized sports betting happening across the country. However, Manfred denied both requests, pointing to the Veteran’s Committee for any Hall of Fame discussions regarding Rose. Manfred also shot down any speculation about Rose’s reinstatement in 2023, as the league had partnerships with sportsbooks.

Though he isn't in the Baseball Hall of Fame, the Reds inducted Rose into their own hall of fame in 2016, retiring his No. 14. He made several appearances in MLB ballparks in recent years before his death.

In April 1990, Rose pleaded guilty to two felony counts of filing false federal income returns, covering tax years in 1985 and 1987. He admitted to underreporting more than $300,000 in earnings from personal appearances, autograph sessions, memorabilia sales and horseracing/gambling winnings.

item.title: Shedeur Sanders has become the Angel Reese of the NFL, thanks to his insufferable supporters
item.description: Shedeur Sanders' NFL Draft slide mirrors the Angel Reese playbook as Skip Bayless and Stephen A. Smith turn football criticism into racial controversy.
item.content:encoded:
From Skip Bayless accusing NFL teams of racism after the 2025 NFL Draft to ESPN personalities invoking Colin Kaepernick, the Shedeur Sanders discourse looks awfully familiar to anyone who has followed Angel Reese's career in the WNBA. Criticism, of any sort, is seen as a microaggression.

The Shedeur Sanders experiment and discourse has become toxic. Legitimate football criticism is apparently a microaggression, NFL general managers are supposedly conspiring against a young quarterback, and anyone who questions the former Colorado star's abilities as a quarterback in the NFL risks being branded more than a hater. They're labeled discriminatory.

If Sanders does not get the recognition, playing time or praise fans believe he deserves, those fans scream racism.

That should sound very familiar to the way fans and WNBA media have treated the Angel Reese discourse.

In my opinion, Sanders has become the Angel Reese of the NFL, not necessarily because of anything the athletes themselves have done on the court or field, or in the media, but because of the exhausting victimhood narratives pushed by some of their most devoted supporters.

The similarities are uncanny.

Criticize Sanders' decision-making, pocket presence, pre-draft interviews or news conferences? You're racist.

Question Reese's offensive efficiency, shot selection or how she compares to Caitlin Clark? Prepare for accusations of racial bias.

And heaven forbid you suggest another quarterback deserves an opportunity over Sanders or that Clark is simply a better, more exciting basketball player.

For certain corners of sports social media, everything must be viewed through a racial lens. Black versus white. Oppressor versus oppressed. Victim versus villain. They're obsessed with race.

It's exhausting, and some prominent sports media personalities have helped pour gasoline on the fire.

COLIN KAEPERNICK SAYS NFL IS 'ACTIVELY BLACKBALLING ME' 10 YEARS AFTER KNEELING PROTEST BEGAN

Remember when Sanders inexplicably fell to the fifth round of the 2025 NFL Draft?

The Cleveland Browns eventually selected him with the 144th overall pick, despite considerable pre-draft hype that once placed him in the conversation as a first-round election.

Rather than consider that NFL franchises might have legitimate concerns about Sanders' talent, personality, football IQ, work ethic, maturity, or overall fit, some of the biggest names in sports media immediately began suggesting something more sinister.

ESPN's Stephen A. Smith was among the loudest.

KAEPERNICK TELLS 'THE VIEW' THAT NFL OWNERS KEPT HIM OUT OVER POLITICS AND POWER, CLAIMS THEY DONATE TO TRUMP

As Sanders continued falling down draft boards, Smith suggested the situation resembled the NFL's controversial treatment of former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick.

Smith declared, "This feels like (Colin) Kaepernick-level collusion."

He also accused NFL owners of appearing to collude against Sanders and suggested teams were motivated by their dislike of his father, Deion Sanders.

Think about that.

Thirty-two NFL franchises making their own personnel decisions somehow became evidence of a coordinated effort to keep Sanders down, in part because of his race, allegedly.

And Smith wasn't alone.

Skip Bayless initially described Sanders' draft slide as the most disgusting development in NFL Draft history. Then, following Sanders' impressive preseason debut against the Carolina Panthers in August 2025, Bayless took things considerably further.

"Tonight, Shedeur Sanders made the entire National Football League look like a whole bunch of petty fools and, in some cases, racist fools."

Bayless also accused teams of being motivated by their dislike of Deion Sanders, arguing that Shedeur had embarrassed the organizations that passed on him.

There was just one glaring problem: Bayless didn't provide evidence establishing that any NFL team passed on Sanders because of his race.

Apparently, one strong preseason performance was enough to expose an alleged league-wide racial conspiracy.

Former ESPN analyst Ryan Clark also brought race into the conversation before the draft, suggesting that Sanders faced additional scrutiny because he was a confident Black quarterback, something many Sanders fans have echoed online throughout the last two seasons.

Clark argued that Sanders' appearance, bravado, and skin color contributed to the criticism surrounding him.

They willfully chose to ignore the legitimate football-related explanations for his slide and pushed the black victim narrative.

CBS Sports NFL insider Jonathan Jones reported concerns about how Sanders handled the pre-draft process, while other reporting highlighted questions surrounding his interviews, preparation, and ability to transition to the professional game.

Former NFL quarterback Boomer Esiason even reported that some teams had removed Sanders from their draft boards entirely.

Could NFL teams have misjudged Sanders? Sure.

Could they have overreacted to his personality or the attention surrounding his famous father? Plausible.

But being evaluated incorrectly isn't automatically discrimination. Sometimes teams simply don't believe a player is worth the investment, especially in the early rounds.

That's how the NFL Draft works.

If you've followed the WNBA since Caitlin Clark and Angel Reese entered the league, you've already watched a similar spectacle unfold.

Clark and Reese have been linked since their memorable college basketball battles, but some supporters have transformed their rivalry into something far more divisive than basketball.

For certain Reese defenders, criticism of her offensive game, including mentioning her uncanny ability to rebound her own misses, humorously trademarking "MeBounds," is treated not merely as an opinion about basketball skill, but as a potential indictment of the critic's racial attitudes.

Meanwhile, praise for Clark can become entangled in arguments about racial privilege and the treatment of Black women in professional sports.

ESPN's Monica McNutt helped illustrate just how quickly the conversation can shift.

Following Clark's flagrant foul against Reese in May 2025, McNutt discussed allegations of racist fan behavior and questioned how differently the incident would have been received had Reese committed the foul.

McNutt argued that the two athletes were being placed into opposing roles, with one portrayed as a victim and the other as someone needing protection.

Her comments were part of a broader discussion about racial double standards, but they also demonstrated how quickly a basketball play can become a referendum on race.

The race card is pulled in almost every controversial play and action Reese has been involved in.

The controversy became even more revealing when the WNBA investigated allegations of hateful fan comments and "monkey noises" directed toward Reese during that same Fever vs Sky game.

The league ultimately announced that its investigation could not substantiate the specific allegations.

Even WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert found herself under fire in September 2024 when she discussed the commercial appeal of the Clark-Reese rivalry without initially delivering the condemnation of racist fan behavior that several players and the players' union wanted.

The backlash was substantial, with prominent players including DiJonai Carrington criticizing her response. Engelbert subsequently clarified that racism and hatred had no place in the league.

More often than not, situations involving Angel Reese have become a racial grievance. It's nauseating.

And now we have the Dillon Gabriel vs Shedeur Sanders situation.

Sanders and Gabriel entered the Cleveland Browns' quarterback room under dramatically different circumstances. Gabriel was selected in the third round of the 2025 NFL Draft, while Sanders had to wait until the fifth.

For some Sanders supporters, that draft order itself became another reason to question whether the NFL was treating their favorite quarterback fairly based on race.

The rivalry has also provided endless ammunition for social media arguments about which quarterback deserves opportunities and whether Cleveland has handled Sanders appropriately.

Instead of allowing Gabriel and Sanders to compete as quarterbacks based on meritocracy, some fans seemed determined to make their competition about something bigger.

Every compliment directed toward Gabriel becomes a potential slight against Sanders. Every criticism of Sanders becomes an opportunity to question the motivations of coaches, executives, or media members.

It's the same exhausting dynamic surrounding Clark and Reese.

Rather than simply acknowledging that two athletes have different strengths, weaknesses, and accomplishments, some supporters insist on turning the conversation into a moral crusade.

Here's what makes this entire controversy so ridiculous: Shedeur Sanders and Angel Reese don't need these narratives to justify their places in professional sports.

Sanders was a productive college quarterback who earned an opportunity in the NFL. Reese became a national champion at LSU and established herself as a formidable rebounder, and many times this season, an effective scorer in the WNBA.

Their accomplishments are legitimate, but so are criticisms of their games.

Sanders can be a talented quarterback who still has weaknesses that NFL coaches and GMs must evaluate. Reese can be an outstanding rebounder whose offensive efficiency deserves scrutiny. Neither observation is inherently racist. Neither athlete needs supporters inventing ulterior motives every time someone offers an unfavorable assessment.

The irony is that the constant racial framing can ultimately undermine the very athletes their fans claim to defend.

Instead of discussing Sanders' development as a quarterback, we're debating whether NFL executives are racists. Instead of discussing Reese's rebounding, scoring, or defensive impact, we're debating whether someone praising Clark is participating in racial favoritism. It's a disservice to both athletes.

And when media personalities with enormous platforms amplify accusations without presenting sufficient evidence, they make the discourse even worse. Sports fans should be able to criticize players without being subjected to a trial over their character. They should be able to support Gabriel, or in this season's case, Deshaun Watson, without hating Sanders, or celebrate Clark without harboring animosity toward Reese.

Actual racism deserves condemnation. Actual discrimination deserves investigation. But disagreement is not discrimination, criticism is not persecution, and losing a competition is not proof of a conspiracy.

Unfortunately, that's a message some of the loudest Sanders and Reese supporters desperately need to hear.

Because the more they insist that every setback is evidence of racial injustice, the more they turn two accomplished athletes into perpetual victims in a culture war neither needs to win.

When I see Sanders fans in my replies say things like, "ANY black athlete that has confidence and swagger makes white nationalist males uncomfortable I’m starting to see," I immediately roll my eyes. These fans can't understand that Shedeur may come across to many people as immature, self-absorbed at times, and lacking self-awareness when he seemingly disrespects the Saints defense when he's about to make his first start of the season.

Disagree all you want, but his actions, including his arrogance he's displayed at times, along with his play are why so many teams passed on him in the NFL Draft.

Let this sink in. Out of 42 eligible quarterback last season, Shedeur Sanders ranked 41st in Passer Rating. He threw more interceptions than touchdowns. He had the fifth-worst QBR since QBR became a stat in 2006, making it the worst for any Browns QB with at least six starts in the history of the franchise.

My criticism is not racism. I could lay out why I believe Watson is the best option as starter for the Cleveland Browns, but we'll save that for another article. All in all, my thoughts are based on what I see on the field and my opinion of what I hear from him off of it, which seems to be echoed by NFL front office and some media members.

The stats don't lie. You supporter do.

item.title: NYU professor, podcaster says he 'took a giant dump' in his Tesla before selling it due to anger at Elon Musk
item.description: Scott Galloway said he took a "giant dump" in his Tesla's passenger seat before selling it as a protest against Elon Musk's online behavior.
item.content:encoded:
NYU professor and host of the "Pivot" podcast Scott Galloway claimed before a live audience on Sunday that he defecated in his own Tesla vehicle before selling it, describing the act as personal payback after tech billionaire and Tesla CEO Elon Musk repeatedly targeted him online.

"As a true story. I had a Tesla. Great car. He started sh---posting me on Twitter, so I sold it," Galloway told co-host Kara Swisher during a live taping at the Orpheum Theatre in Los Angeles. "Not before taking a giant dump in the passenger seat. True story. Not good for resale value."

Fox News Digital reached out to Elon Musk and Tesla for comment.

ELON MUSK’S AUSTIN HOME TARGETED BY WELL-FUNDED LEFTIST GROUPS ABOARD PARTY BUSES

The admission came during a discussion about the midterm results, Musk's political power and reports that Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production in Texas in mid-2027. Despite Democrats dominating the elections, Swisher and Galloway lamented how much political influence and power Musk continues to have.

Musk, once a darling of liberal commentators for popularizing electric vehicles, has faced mounting scrutiny from the left since purchasing Twitter, now X, becoming an outspoken conservative supporter and emerging as a political megadonor.

"We have become out of control in terms of one man — a private citizen's ability to control the government and make decisions that only elected officials should be allowed to make," Galloway said. 

Swisher agreed, calling Musk "a cartoon villain."

NEW BOOK ON ELON MUSK EXAMINES THE BILLIONAIRE’S MIND, MOTIVATION AND MAKING LIFE MULTI-PLANETARY

"No individual should have — and he is not elected. He is unaccountable, and he should work on his — not the cyber truck obviously, because that was a sh---- product," Swisher said. "But he should work on those kind of things and not have this — it would be a really good thing for him and for the rest of us for him to go away for a while, get off Twitter and stop talking."

On election day, Galloway had laid out an alternate history scenario on his "Prof G Podcast" to draw a comparison between Musk's actions and a hypothetical World War II scenario involving aviator Charles Lindbergh. Galloway was referring to reports that SpaceX restricted Starlink satellite internet speeds in Ukraine last month, reportedly disrupting Ukrainian military operations during the country's war with Russia. He made the case that Musk should be treated like traitors who had collaborated with a foreign enemy.

"My question is, or my thesis is, we took the Rosenbergs and put them up against a wall and executed them for being traitors. And I realize this is an incendiary statement, but I'll make it, and I believe it. I think Elon Musk is a traitor to the West," he said.

Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were executed in 1953 after being convicted of conspiracy to commit espionage for the Soviet Union in a case involving U.S. atomic secrets.

Musk explained the Starlink controversy by saying Ukraine was using it in violation of the service's restrictions, saying, "Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be."
